main.summary: The Classic of Purity and Stillness teaches that purity and stillness are the root of attaining the Dao. Heaven and earth are by nature pure and turbid, moving and still; a person who sets desire aside and clears the mind, seeing emptiness without clinging even to emptiness, returns to the true and constant Way. Three appended notes, by Ge Xuan and two other Daoist immortals, urge readers to recite it.
main.translation:
Laozi said: The great Dao has no form, yet it gives birth to heaven and earth. The great Dao has no feeling, yet it sets the sun and moon in motion. The great Dao has no name, yet it nourishes the ten thousand things. I do not know its name, so I force myself to call it Dao.
Now the Dao has the pure and the turbid, the moving and the still. Heaven is pure and earth is turbid; heaven moves and earth is still; the male is pure and the female is turbid; the male moves and the female is still. Descending from the root and flowing out to the branch tips, it gives birth to the ten thousand things. The pure is the source of the turbid; the still is the foundation of the moving. If a person can be constantly pure and still, heaven and earth will all return to him.
The spirit of a person likes purity, but the heart disturbs it. The heart of a person likes stillness, but desire pulls it away. If one can send desire away, the heart becomes still of itself; if one clears the heart, the spirit becomes pure of itself. Then the six desires do not arise and the three poisons are destroyed. Those who cannot do this have not yet cleared the heart and not yet sent desire away.
To send it away, look inward at the heart: the heart has no heart. Look outward at the body: the body has no body. Look far at the things of the world: things have no things. When these three are understood, only emptiness is seen. Look at emptiness, and that too is empty; emptiness has nothing left to be empty about. When there is nothing left to be empty, even 'no' is no more. When even 'no' is no more, all is deep and calm, forever still. When stillness has nothing left to be still, how can desire arise? When desire no longer arises, that is true stillness. True stillness answers to things, true constancy keeps its nature. Always answering and always still: this is constant purity and stillness.
With such purity and stillness one gradually enters the true Way. Having entered the true Way, one is said to have attained the Dao. Yet although we say 'attained the Dao', in truth nothing is attained; it is only in order to teach living beings that it is called attaining the Dao. One who can understand this may pass on the sacred Way.
Laozi said: The highest sort of person does not contend; the lowest sort loves to contend. The highest virtue does not think itself virtuous; the lowest virtue clings to virtue. Those who cling cannot be said to have the Dao or virtue.
The reason living beings do not find the true Way is that they have a deluded mind. Once there is a deluded mind, the spirit is startled. Once the spirit is startled, one becomes attached to the ten thousand things. Once attached to the ten thousand things, craving and seeking arise. Once craving and seeking arise, there are troubles. Troubles and deluded thoughts weigh down body and heart with sorrow and pain. Then one meets defilement and disgrace, drifts through birth and death, sinks for ever in the sea of suffering, and loses the true Way for good. The Way of the true and constant is found, of itself, by the one who awakens to it. One who has awakened to the Way is constantly pure and still.
The immortal Ge Xuan said: I attained the true Way, and I once recited this classic ten thousand times. This classic is practised by the heavenly beings and is not handed down to lesser people. In the past I received it from the Lord of the Eastern Flower; the Lord of the Eastern Flower received it from the Lord of the Golden Gate Tower; the Lord of the Golden Gate Tower received it from the Queen Mother of the West. The Queen Mother of the West always passed it on by mouth and never put it into writing. Now I have written it down in the world. The highest sort of person who understands it will rise to be an officer of heaven. The middle sort who practises it will be ranked among the immortals of the Southern Palace. The lowest sort who obtains it will live long in this world, roam the three realms and ascend through the golden gate.
The Perfected One of the Left Mystery said: One who studies the Way and keeps up recitation of this classic will be guarded by the good spirits of the ten heavens. Then jade talismans will protect his spirit and the golden elixir will refine his body; body and spirit will both become wondrous, and he will join the Dao in truth.
The Perfected One of Orthodox Unity said: In a household that has this classic, one who understands it will not be troubled by disaster or hindrance; the holy ones will guard the gate, and the spirit will rise to the higher realms to pay homage to the exalted ones. When merit is complete and virtue achieved, there will be a response from the Lords above. If one keeps reciting and does not fall back, the body will rise on purple clouds.

glossary.note: Purity means a mind that is clear and untroubled; stillness means not being stirred by outer things. The whole classic takes 'constant purity and stillness' as the master principle of cultivating the Dao.

glossary.en: liuyu, sandu - the six desires and the three poisons
glossary.note: The six desires are the desires that arise through the six senses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind); another reading takes them as the desires of life, death, ears, eyes, mouth and nose. The three poisons are borrowed from Buddhism: greed, anger and delusion. Here they stand for all harmful states of mind.

glossary.en: neiguan, waiguan, yuanguan - looking inward, outward and far
glossary.note: In turn one looks at the mind, the body and external things, until 'the heart has no heart, the body has no body, things have no things'. This is the classic's method of practice, close to letting go of clinging to 'self' and to 'things'.

glossary.en: wuwu yi wu - even 'no' is no more
glossary.note: Even 'nothing' is not to be held as real. The idea echoes Zhuangzi, and the Buddhist-Daoist habit of letting go of both sides: clinging to emptiness or to non-being must be put down as well.

glossary.en: shangde bu de, xiade zhi de - the highest virtue does not think itself virtuous, the lowest clings to virtue
glossary.note: This comes from chapter 38 of the Daodejing. A person of the highest virtue follows the natural way and does not count himself virtuous, and so has virtue; a person of lower virtue deliberately holds on to virtue, and so does not have the real thing.
A concept found in both Daoism and Buddhism. Daoism often means the realms of desire, form and formlessness, and it is sometimes read as heaven, the human world and the underworld.

glossary.term: 葛玄、左玄真人、正一真人
glossary.en: Ge Xuan, Zuoxuan zhenren, Zhengyi zhenren - Ge Xuan and two Perfected Ones
glossary.note: All are figures of Daoist tradition. Ge Xuan lived in the Wu kingdom of the Three Kingdoms period and is honoured as the 'Immortal of the Great Ultimate'. The Perfected One of the Left Mystery and the Perfected One of Orthodox Unity are immortals named in the closing notes, which lend the classic sacred authority and a line of transmission.

main.background: Tradition attributes this classic to Laozi, honoured in Daoism as the Supreme Venerable Lord (Taishang Laojun). It seems in fact to have been put together between the late Tang dynasty (618-907) and the Five Dynasties (907-960), and it became widely read after Du Guangting wrote a commentary on it. The Quanzhen school of Daoism made it part of its morning and evening devotions. The text joins Laozi's idea of 'purity, stillness and non-action' with the Buddhist method of 'contemplating emptiness'. The last three paragraphs (by Ge Xuan and the two Perfected Ones) were added by later hands and are not part of the main text.
